title: Local n8n
dek: Four commands put a working automation server on your own machine. This is what each one does, why the defaults in most guides will lose your work, and how to fix it when it stops.
summary: Installing and running n8n locally on a Mac, with the mental model first.

blocks.html: Say it's this: every weekday at 7am, pull yesterday's orders out of a spreadsheet, add them up, and post the total to Slack. Ten seconds of work. Ten seconds you do three hundred times a year, and forget twice a month.
n8n is a tool for building that once and letting it run. You lay out the steps on a canvas, connect them with lines, and it fires on whatever schedule you give it.

You can rent it. This runs it on your own machine instead — free, and your spreadsheet credentials never leave your disk. The trade is that it only runs while the machine is awake, which we come back to at the end when you have enough context to judge whether that's a dealbreaker.
Hold on to the 7am Slack job. Every piece below exists to serve it, and we build a stripped-down version of it further down.

You can install this by pasting commands you don't understand — plenty of guides work that way. But two of the four commands contain a flag that decides whether your work survives next month, and you can't see which unless you hold the model first. It takes about two minutes.

blocks.text: One · A workflow is a chain of steps

blocks.html: Each step is called a node. The first node decides when the chain runs — a time of day, an incoming message, a button. Every node after it decides what happens, and hands its result to the next one along the wire.
Our 7am job is four nodes: a schedule, a spreadsheet read, a sum, a Slack post. That's the whole shape of n8n, and it doesn't get more complicated as jobs get bigger — just longer.

blocks.text: Two · It runs inside a sealed box

blocks.html: Rather than installing n8n onto your Mac directly, you run it inside a container — a sealed box holding the program and every version of every dependency it needs. Nothing inside can collide with anything you already have, and deleting the box leaves no residue.

The sealed-box picture is worth holding, but here is where it stops being exact: a container isn't a second computer. It shares your Mac's operating system core rather than booting its own. That's why it starts in about a second instead of the minute a virtual machine would take, and why it costs almost nothing to leave running.

Something has to run these boxes. On a Mac that's OrbStack — lighter and faster than Docker Desktop on Apple Silicon, and it understands the same docker commands, so every Docker instruction you find online still applies.

blocks.text: Three · Your work does not live in the box

blocks.html: This is the idea that saves you, and the one most quick-start guides skip.
The container is disposable on purpose. You throw it away and rebuild it every time you update n8n — that is the update procedure. So if your workflows lived inside it, updating would delete them.
They don't, because you point the container at a volume: a patch of storage that sits outside the box and stays put when the box is destroyed. Your workflows, credentials and run history live there.

blocks.caption: The line between them is a single flag — -v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n — which appears in the install command below. It reads: mount the volume called n8n_data at the place inside the box where n8n writes its files. Leave it out and n8n writes into the box instead, where it looks fine until the first rebuild.

blocks.html: You need macOS 14 or newer, about 3 GB free, and Homebrew — the command-line installer for Mac software. Check for it with brew --version. A version number means you're ready; command not found means start at brew.sh and come back.

blocks.text: Plate 01 · Install the thing that runs boxes

blocks.html: OrbStack, from above. It will ask for your Mac password partway through, because it installs a privileged networking helper. The characters won't appear as you type — that's normal for a password prompt in a terminal, not a frozen screen.

lines.text: start it, give it 20s, then ask the engine to identify itself

blocks.html: You should see a long block of version text that includes a Server: Docker Engine section. If you only get client information plus an error about a daemon, OrbStack hasn't finished waking up. Wait ten seconds and run docker version again.

blocks.text: Plate 02 · Create the storage, then the container

blocks.html: Two commands, in this order. The first makes the volume; the second downloads n8n and starts it with that volume attached.

lines.text: the storage that outlives the container

blocks.html: Four parts of that command are worth reading rather than pasting blind:

head: Flag
What it does, and what happens without it
rows: Runs n8n in the background. Without it, n8n holds your terminal window open and dies when you close it.
Publishes the box's port 5678 to your Mac, which is what makes localhost:5678 reachable. Without it, n8n runs but nothing can see it.
The volume from above. Without it, every workflow you build dies with the container.
Brings n8n back after a reboot. It has a sharp edge, covered below.

blocks.title: Set your timezone first
blocks.label: Change this before you run the command
blocks.html:
Replace both instances of Asia/Kolkata with your own — Europe/London, America/New_York, whatever applies. These two variables are the reason a workflow scheduled for 7am fires at your 7am rather than somewhere else's.

Our example job is a 7am job. Get this wrong and it silently becomes a 1:30am job.
The first run downloads roughly 500 MB, so give it a minute or two. When the prompt comes back, check what's running:
One line, status Up, port mapped. That's a working install.
Open localhost:5678. The word localhost means this machine and nowhere else — the page isn't published to the internet, and nobody outside your Mac can reach it.

blocks.alt: The n8n owner account setup form with fields for email, first name, last name and password.
blocks.caption: This account exists only on your disk, so the email is never verified and never mailed — but it is your username, so pick a real one. The password needs eight characters, one number, one capital.

blocks.html: A 7am job is worthless if the thing running it quietly died on Tuesday. So it's worth knowing exactly what brings n8n back, and the one case where it deliberately won't. Three things have to be alive, and each one starts the next.

blocks.html: That leaves one link doing more work than it looks: OrbStack has to launch itself at login. If it doesn't, layer 2 never starts, and a restart policy with no engine to enforce it does nothing at all. Open OrbStack's settings and confirm Start at login is ticked. It's the cheapest reliability you'll buy today.
What it is: a standing instruction to the engine — if this container isn't running, start it.
Why you want it: without it, every reboot leaves n8n switched off until you notice, and a 7am job that needs you to remember something at 6:55 isn't automation.

Where it bites: read the words literally. The engine restarts the container unless you stopped it yourself. Run docker stop n8n and the engine records that as a deliberate decision and respects it — through the next reboot, and every reboot after that, indefinitely.

What people get wrong: they assume "restart" means "always restart", stop the container to quiet it down for an afternoon, reboot a few days later, and conclude the install is broken. It isn't. It's obeying an instruction they forgot they gave. The cure is one word: docker start n8n.

blocks.title: When the page won't load
blocks.label: Run this before diagnosing anything
blocks.html:
open -a OrbStack && docker start n8n

It covers both failure modes at once — engine not running, container not running — and it's safe when things are already up, because starting something that's already started does nothing.

If that doesn't do it, docker ps -a tells you whether the container is Up or Exited, and docker logs n8n puts the reason in the last few lines. A daemon connection error from either command means you're missing layer 2, not layer 3.

Back to the 7am Slack job. It's four nodes, two of which need account credentials — so before wiring those up, build the two-node skeleton that proves the machinery works. Same shape, nothing to connect, about a minute.

blocks.alt: The n8n trigger panel listing Trigger manually, On app event, On a schedule, On webhook call and other options.
blocks.caption: Click Build a workflow, then Add first step. The real job would take On a schedule. Take Trigger manually instead, so it runs only when you press the button and you can watch it work.

blocks.alt: The Edit Fields node with an empty name field, a String type dropdown, and an empty value field.
blocks.caption: Press +, search Edit Fields. In the real job this position holds the spreadsheet read. Edit Fields just invents a piece of data, which is exactly what you want when testing — no account, no credentials, no chance of emailing anyone.

blocks.alt: The Edit Fields node after running, showing output containing a greeting field.
blocks.caption: Hit Execute step. The output panel fills in on the right. What you see there is precisely what the next node would receive — which is how you debug a chain that isn't behaving.

blocks.alt: The n8n canvas showing a manual trigger connected to an Edit Fields node, both outlined in green, with a 1 item label on the connecting line.
blocks.caption: Green outlines mean both nodes ran. The 1 item on the wire is the data crossing between them. Your 7am job is this picture with four nodes instead of two.

blocks.html: To finish the real thing: swap the manual trigger for On a schedule set to 07:00, and replace Edit Fields with Google Sheets, then a Code or Summarize node, then Slack. The two account nodes will ask you to sign in the first time and store the token in the volume. Check Templates in the sidebar first — a spreadsheet-to-Slack digest is common enough that a starting point already exists.

head: Operation
Command
rows: docker stop n8n — remember: this survives reboots
docker logs -f n8n — Ctrl+C stops watching, not the container
docker pull n8nio/n8n → docker stop n8n && docker rm n8n → re-run the run command
docker stop n8n && docker rm n8n → docker volume rm n8n_data — the second command cannot be undone

blocks.html: The update row is the model in practice: destroy the container, build a new one from the newer image, and the volume it reattaches to still holds everything. The backup row mounts your volume and your Desktop into a throwaway container and tars one into the other — worth running before any update, and worth keeping somewhere that isn't this laptop.

head: Symptom
Cause, and what to do
rows: Cannot connect to the Docker daemon
Layer 2 is down. open -a OrbStack, wait twenty seconds, try again.
Run docker ps. Not listed → docker start n8n. Listed but blank → docker logs n8n, and the reason is in the last few lines.
Something else on your Mac holds 5678. Change the left number only — -p 5679:5678 — then use localhost:5679. The right number is inside the box and never changes.
Scheduled jobs fire at the wrong hour
Timezone. Remove the container and re-run the run command with the correct GENERIC_TIMEZONE and TZ. Your workflows are in the volume, so nothing is lost.
It was started without -v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n, so n8n had nowhere permanent to write. Unfortunately the earlier work is gone.
Name n8n is already in use
An old container is still around. docker rm -f n8n, then re-run. Safe, for the same reason the update is safe.

blocks.title: Carry this
blocks.label: Everything else you can look up
blocks.html:
A workflow is a chain of nodes. The first says when, the rest say what.

n8n runs in a container, and the container is disposable — you replace it to update.

Your work lives in the volume, not the container, which is the only reason replacing it is safe.

OrbStack starts the container, and only if OrbStack itself starts. Everything you'll ever debug is one of those two not running.

The honest limit: this sleeps when your Mac sleeps. Close the lid and the 7am job doesn't fire. That's fine for anything you trigger yourself and fatal for anything genuinely unattended — which is the moment people move to a small always-on machine or a rented instance. Nothing about that migration wastes what you've done here; it's the same container and the same volume, somewhere that stays awake.

The licence allows this. n8n's Sustainable Use License permits free self-hosting for your own internal business purposes. What it prohibits is reselling n8n — white-labelling it, or hosting it as a paid service for other people.
